meta.title: Swahili A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Swahili → English (see the Swahili, recall the meaning) and English → Swahili (see an English meaning, recall the Swahili). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Swahili that could be used here, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 277 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words and little words every sentence is built out of — and the other 223 are the commonest remaining words, counted by the WHOLE word (every form of a noun, every conjugated form of a verb added together) in two collections of real Swahili, film and television subtitles and the Global Voices news site, a word having to be common in both. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Verbs are shown as their infinitive (kusoma, to read) with their stem (-soma), which every tense is built on, and their negative infinitive; adjectives and possessives as their stem (-zuri, -angu) with the forms they take after three of the noun classes. The 231 nouns show their class, which every adjective, verb and possessive agrees with, and their plural; there are 122 verbs. Real example sentences come with 482 of the 500 words, three apiece for 459 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, noun classes and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: counted from OpenSubtitles 2024 and Global Voices (CC BY 3.0), both as distributed by OPUS. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
